subject: PHS
subtopic: Challenging patient and ethical scenarios: error disclosure, safety, special situations
vignette: A 58-year-old man undergoes an upper endoscopy at a busy outpatient center. Later that evening, the team discovers that a mucosal biopsy intended for another patient was mistakenly taken from him. The specimen shows benign gastric mucosa, and he has no complication. He calls the next day asking why he has a sore throat and a bruise on his hand. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: I am sorry to tell you that a biopsy intended for another patient was mistakenly taken from you; regardless of the benign result, you deserved to know, and we will discuss what happens next.
Because the tissue was completely normal and you suffered no harm, there is nothing that needs to be disclosed to you.
I have noted the event in your chart, and we will contact you only if anything abnormal is ever found in the specimen.
You will need to file a formal complaint or legal claim before we can give you any details about what happened.
Your sore throat and hand bruise are routine effects of your scheduled procedure, and there is nothing further to discuss.

explanation_correct: Regardless of the outcome, a physician is ethically obligated to inform a patient that a mistake has been made. The benign result and the absence of complications do not eliminate this duty. The appropriate response is prompt, honest disclosure with an apology and a discussion of next steps, which supports the principles of autonomy and nonmaleficence and maintains trust.

explanation_incorrect.B: A good outcome does not excuse silence; the obligation to disclose a mistake exists regardless of whether the patient was harmed.
explanation_incorrect.C: Silently documenting the error and waiting for an abnormality to surface withholds the disclosure the patient is ethically owed.
explanation_incorrect.D: Conditioning disclosure on a legal or formal complaint is improper; the duty to inform exists independently of any claim the patient may file.
explanation_incorrect.E: Describing the event as a routine effect of his own scheduled procedure is deceptive and denies the patient knowledge of a mistake made on his body.

educationalObjective: When an invasive test is performed on the wrong patient, disclose the error to the patient regardless of the outcome or the presence of harm.

subject: PHS
subtopic: Challenging patient and ethical scenarios: error disclosure, safety, special situations
vignette: A 7-year-old boy's 9-year-old sister died of leukemia 3 weeks ago. Since then he has been withdrawn and tearful. He asks his pediatrician, 'Did my sister die because I teased her? Is she coming back when she gets better?' Which of the following is the most appropriate response?
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Your sister has gone to a beautiful place where she is happy and will always be watching over you.
Your sister is just sleeping now, and her body is still here, so she has not really left us.
You are too young to understand death, so let's wait until you are older to talk about it.
Do not worry — nobody blames you, and I am sure you will feel happy again very soon.
When someone dies, their body stops working forever and they cannot come back; your sister's death was not caused by anything you did, and it is normal to feel sad and scared.

explanation_correct: At ages 5–7, children begin to understand that death is permanent, that all life functions end completely at death, and that everything alive eventually dies. The appropriate response gives a direct, concrete description of the sister's death, avoids clichés and euphemisms, reassures the boy that he is not responsible, and identifies and normalizes his fears and feelings. Option E accomplishes all of these.

explanation_incorrect.A: 'Gone to a beautiful place' is a euphemism that avoids a direct, concrete description of death and can leave a child in this age group confused about what happened.
explanation_incorrect.B: Telling a child that the body 'is still here' and she is 'not really gone' is a cliché that contradicts the concept of death's permanence and may make the boy fear going to sleep himself.
explanation_incorrect.C: Children ages 5–7 do begin to understand death as permanent, so deferring the conversation avoids giving the concrete explanation and reassurance he needs now.
explanation_incorrect.D: Although the reassurance about responsibility is good, this response offers no direct explanation of death, dismisses his feelings with a promise of quick happiness, and does not normalize grief.

educationalObjective: For grieving children ages 5–7, explain death concretely as permanent, avoid euphemisms, reassure them they are not responsible, and normalize their feelings.

subject: PHS
subtopic: Challenging patient and ethical scenarios: error disclosure, safety, special situations
vignette: A 28-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her boyfriend for a 'twisted wrist.' He insists on staying for the entire interview and answers most questions for her. Radiographs show no fracture, but examination reveals bruises in various stages of healing on her arms and torso. When he steps out to take a phone call, she says quietly, 'Please don't make this a big deal.' Which of the following is the most appropriate response?
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: I am legally required to report your boyfriend to the police immediately, and an officer will come speak with you now.
You must leave this relationship today; I can give you the number of a local shelter so you can arrange to move out.
If you are unwilling to tell me how you really got these bruises, I cannot responsibly treat your wrist.
Thank you for letting me know something is wrong; are you safe at home right now, and would you like to make a plan for what you would do in an emergency?
I will document in your chart that the injuries were accidental so that your boyfriend is not questioned when you come back.

explanation_correct: For a patient who is a victim of intimate partner violence, the physician should ask if the patient is safe and help devise an emergency plan if there is not one. The physician should ask direct, open-ended questions about exam findings and summarize the patient's answers back to her. The physician should not necessarily pressure the patient to leave her partner or disclose the incident to the authorities, unless required by state law. Option D does exactly this while validating her disclosure.

explanation_incorrect.A: Calling the police immediately is premature; reporting is required only when state law mandates it, and the first step is assessing safety and planning, not alerting authorities against her wishes.
explanation_incorrect.B: Pressuring the patient to leave her partner immediately is inappropriate; the physician supports autonomy by assessing safety and offering resources without issuing demands.
explanation_incorrect.C: Making treatment conditional on disclosure is coercive; care should be provided regardless, and the patient should not be punished for her hesitancy.
explanation_incorrect.E: Deliberately falsifying the medical record to conceal evidence is dishonest, undermines her safety plan, and is never an appropriate way to protect a patient.

educationalObjective: For intimate partner violence, assess safety, create an emergency plan, and use open-ended questions without pressuring the patient to leave the partner or report unless state law requires it.

subject: PHS
subtopic: Challenging patient and ethical scenarios: error disclosure, safety, special situations
vignette: At 8:00 AM, a colleague arrives to begin seeing clinic patients. You notice he is unsteady on his feet, his speech is slurred, and he smells of alcohol. When you mention it, he says, 'I'm fine — just one drink last night — do not make a fuss.' Which of the following is the most appropriate response?
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: I will quietly cover his patients myself until he feels more alert, and we will not need to involve anyone else.
I will tell him to take a long break and resume seeing patients in the afternoon once he is sober.
I will ensure he is removed from patient care and report the situation through the appropriate channels so that he can receive help and patients are protected.
I will confront him in front of the medical team so that everyone knows he has a drinking problem before he harms someone.
I will wait to see whether this happens again before taking any action, since a single incident may be a misunderstanding.

explanation_correct: An impaired physician presents a potential risk to patient safety. There is an ethical and usually a legal obligation to report impaired colleagues so that they can cease patient care and receive appropriate assistance in a timely manner. Reporting should follow institutional procedures, with guidance sought as applicable law varies by institution and state. Option C removes him from care and routes the report through proper channels.

explanation_incorrect.A: Informally covering his patients leaves an impaired colleague available to return to clinical duties and bypasses the reporting obligation; patients remain at risk.
explanation_incorrect.B: Letting him resume patient care later the same day leaves the impaired state unaddressed and does not ensure he receives assistance.
explanation_incorrect.D: Publicly confronting and exposing the colleague humiliates him and bypasses institutional channels; the goal is reporting through proper procedures, not shaming in front of the team.
explanation_incorrect.E: Waiting for a repeat event delays removing an actively impaired physician from patient care and endangers patients seen today.

educationalObjective: Report impaired colleagues through appropriate channels so they cease patient care and receive help; this is an ethical and usually a legal obligation.

subject: PHS
subtopic: Challenging patient and ethical scenarios: error disclosure, safety, special situations
vignette: A 24-year-old man was declared brain dead 2 days after a motor vehicle collision, with absent brainstem reflexes and a positive apnea test. His parents refuse to accept this and say, 'Look, he squeezed our hands and turned toward us when we touched him. He is still alive, and you must keep him on the ventilator.' Which of the following is the most appropriate response?
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Brain death is death, and there is no chance of recovery; the movements are spinal reflexes rather than signs of consciousness, and I will bring this case to the ethics committee to address the futility of continued life support.
We will continue full ventilatory support for as long as your family wishes, since only the family can decide when care has become futile.
Because he has been moving, we should repeat the brain death examination several more times before reaching any conclusion.
I will ask the hospital attorney to seek a court order to disconnect the ventilator immediately over your objection.
We will transfer him to another facility that may be able to offer experimental treatments for his brain injury.

explanation_correct: Brain death is equivalent to death, and there is no chance of recovery. Movements after brain death are due to spinal arc reflexes and are not voluntary. The physician should gently explain this to the family and bring the case to the appropriate ethics board regarding the futility of care and withdrawal of life support. Option A pairs the explanation with the proper escalation pathway.

explanation_incorrect.B: Indefinite support of a brain-dead patient at the family's insistence provides physiologically futile care; the ethics committee pathway, not unbounded family discretion, is the appropriate next step.
explanation_incorrect.C: Repeating the examination is unnecessary because brain death has already been declared; the observed movements are spinal arc reflexes, not evidence of recovery.
explanation_incorrect.D: Skipping straight to legal action is adversarial and abandons the required step of gentle explanation and ethics review before any unilateral move to withdraw support.
explanation_incorrect.E: Transferring a brain-dead patient for 'experimental treatment' is medically futile and misleads the family about the possibility of recovery.

educationalObjective: Brain death equals death; postmortem movements are spinal reflexes, so explain this to the family gently and refer disputes about futility to the ethics committee.

subject: PHS
subtopic: Challenging patient and ethical scenarios: error disclosure, safety, special situations
vignette: A 38-year-old woman and her 15-year-old daughter are brought to the emergency department unresponsive and bleeding heavily after a motor vehicle collision. Both are in hemorrhagic shock and require immediate transfusion. The father arrives and says the family are Jehovah's Witnesses, and he refuses transfusion for both of them. There is no documented statement from the mother about her preferences. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Transfuse neither patient, because the father is the healthcare proxy and his refusal is binding for both of them.
Transfuse the daughter, but do not transfuse the mother and respect the proxy's refusal on her behalf.
Transfuse both patients, because a healthcare proxy is never permitted to refuse emergency treatment on a patient's behalf.
Transfuse the mother, but do not transfuse the daughter, because the father's refusal is binding only for adult family members.
Wait for a court order before transfusing either patient, given the urgency of the situation and the religious objection.

explanation_correct: Emergent care can be refused by the healthcare proxy for an adult, particularly when the patient's preferences are known or reasonably inferred — so the mother is not transfused. However, such refusal cannot be applied to a minor based solely on faith — so the daughter, whose life is immediately threatened, is transfused. This distinguishes proxy refusal for a competent adult's known wishes from the limits of proxy authority over a child.

explanation_incorrect.A: Treating the daughter the same as her mother ignores that a faith-based proxy refusal cannot be used to deny a minor lifesaving emergent care.
explanation_incorrect.C: This is overbroad: a proxy may refuse emergent care for an adult when the patient's preferences are known or reasonably inferred, as here with the mother.
explanation_incorrect.D: This gets the rule backwards: proxy refusal binds the adult but cannot be based solely on faith for the minor, who should be transfused.
explanation_incorrect.E: Delaying transfusion of a patient in hemorrhagic shock while awaiting a court order risks her death; the daughter should be transfused immediately without court involvement.

educationalObjective: Emergent care may be refused by proxy for an adult with known or inferred preferences, but not for a minor based solely on the family's faith.

subject: PHS
subtopic: Challenging patient and ethical scenarios: error disclosure, safety, special situations
vignette: An 82-year-old man with moderate dementia is bedbound and lives with his nephew, his primary caretaker. The nephew brings him in for a 'fall from bed.' Examination shows bruises of different ages across his back and torso and a healing fracture of the left forearm. The nephew's account of how the injuries occurred changes during the interview. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Accept the nephew's explanation, since he is the patient's primary caregiver and knows his daily care best.
Accuse the nephew of physical abuse immediately, before any of the findings are documented.
Contact the patient's attorney to determine whether a new guardian should be appointed before taking any other step.

Document the history and examination findings in detail, provide any necessary medical care, and report the reasonable suspicion of abuse to adult protective services while informing the caretaker of the reporting obligation.
Schedule a follow-up visit in one month to see whether the bruises resolve before involving any outside agency.

explanation_correct: When a dependent patient has injuries inconsistent with the caretaker's story, the physician should document a detailed history and physical, provide any necessary medical care, and, if possible and appropriate, interview the patient alone. If suspicion remains, the physician must contact the appropriate agencies — here, adult protective services. Physicians are required by law to report any reasonable suspicion of abuse, neglect, or endangerment, and the caretaker should be informed of this obligation.

explanation_incorrect.A: Accepting a caretaker's shifting account despite bruises of different ages and a healing fracture ignores a reasonable suspicion of abuse that must be documented and reported.
explanation_incorrect.B: Accusations before documentation and reporting are inappropriate; the obligation is to report suspicion to the authorities, not to personally accuse the caretaker at the bedside.
explanation_incorrect.C: Pursuing guardianship through an attorney is not the first step; the legal requirement is to document findings and report reasonable suspicion to protective services.
explanation_incorrect.E: Delaying a month while the patient remains with the suspected abuser endangers him; the law requires reporting of reasonable suspicion now, not after observation.

educationalObjective: For a dependent patient with injuries inconsistent with the caretaker's story, document carefully, provide care, and report reasonable suspicion to protective services as legally required.
